title: Lines in Disguise: Understanding y = mx + b Through a Living Graph
prerequisites: Plotting points using (x, y) coordinates on a Cartesian plane

m.meaning: slope — the rate at which y changes per unit change in x

b.meaning: y-intercept — the value of y when x equals zero

delta_y.meaning: vertical change between two points on the line

delta_x.meaning: horizontal change between the same two points

line.meaning: the graph of y = mx + b

opening_narration:
Alright, let's start with something you already know how to do — plot a point. You've done it a hundred times. You take an x-value, a y-value, put a dot on the grid. Simple. But here's the thing: what if I told you that a single equation — just five symbols, y equals m x plus b — secretly describes every straight line you can draw on a flat surface, except one weird edge case we'll get to later? That's not an exaggeration. Every ramp, every ski slope, every graph of a phone bill charging a flat fee plus a per-minute rate — all of them live inside that one equation.

Now, before I throw the formula at you and say 'memorise this', I want us to actually build it together. Because here's what I've noticed: a lot of people can write y equals mx plus b from memory, but if you ask them why b is where it is, or what would happen if m got bigger, they go quiet. And that's not their fault — it's because the equation got handed to them without the story behind it.

So here's the story. Imagine you're walking along a straight path on a hillside. You take one step to the right — that's your change in x, what we'll call delta x. And as you do, you either go up, go down, or stay flat — that's your change in y, delta x. The ratio of those two changes, delta y divided by delta x, tells you how steep your path is and which direction it tilts. That ratio is m, the slope. Notice I said ratio — it's not just how big the numbers are, it's how they relate to each other.

And b? That's even simpler. It's just asking: when x is zero — when you're standing right at the starting post — how high up are you? That height is b, the y-intercept.

Here's what I want you to hold onto as we go through this lesson: m and b are independent. Changing one doesn't force the other to change. That independence is actually the whole power of the equation. We're going to watch what happens on a real graph when we tweak m, then tweak b, and you're going to predict what happens before I show you. Getting it wrong is fine — that's actually where the learning happens.

Ready? Let's put a line on that graph.

sections.purpose: Show effect of changing b with m fixed — vertical translation; prediction pause; explain why geometrically
sections.new_inference: Increasing b shifts the entire line upward by the same amount without rotating it; decreasing b shifts it downward; the slope (tilt) is unchanged because m is unchanged

sections.purpose: Show effect of changing m with b fixed — pivoting about (0,b); address the misconception about larger m always meaning steeper
sections.new_inference: Changing m rotates the line around the fixed point (0,b); a more positive m tilts the line more steeply upward left-to-right; a negative m tilts it downward; comparing steepness requires comparing |m|, not signed m

sections.purpose: Cover special cases: m=0 gives horizontal line; vertical lines x=c cannot be written as y=mx+b
sections.new_inference: When m=0, delta_y=0 for any delta_x, so y never changes — the line is horizontal; a vertical line has undefined slope because delta_x=0 and division by zero is undefined, placing it outside y=mx+b

worked_problems.problem: A straight line passes through the points (0, -1) and (3, 5). Write the equation of the line in the form y = mx + b.

solution.step1: Identify b directly: the point (0, -1) is on the y-axis, so b = -1.
solution.step2: Calculate slope m using the two points. Δy = 5 - (-1) = 6. Δx = 3 - 0 = 3. m = Δy/Δx = 6/3 = 2.
solution.step3: Substitute m and b into y = mx + b: y = 2x + (-1), which simplifies to y = 2x - 1.

worked_problems.problem: A straight line passes through the points (1, 4) and (3, 10). Write the equation of the line in the form y = mx + b.

solution.step1: Calculate slope m. Δy = 10 - 4 = 6. Δx = 3 - 1 = 2. m = 6/2 = 3.
solution.step2: We do not have the y-intercept directly, so substitute one point and m into y = mx + b. Using (1, 4): 4 = 3(1) + b. Solve: b = 4 - 3 = 1.
solution.step4: Verify with the second point (3, 10): y = 3(3) + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10. Correct.

independent_problems.problem: A line passes through (0, 2) and (4, 6). Write its equation in the form y = mx + b.
A line has equation y = -2x + 5. State its slope, its y-intercept, and whether it rises or falls from left to right.
independent_problems.answer: Slope m = -2 (red); y-intercept b = 5 (teal); the line falls from left to right because m is negative

independent_problems.problem: Line 1 has slope m = 4 and Line 2 has slope m = -7. Which line is steeper, and why?
independent_problems.answer: Line 2 is steeper. Steepness depends on the absolute value of the slope: |4| = 4 and |-7| = 7. Since 7 > 4, Line 2 has a greater steepness even though its slope is negative.

misconception_checks.misconception: Students confuse the y-intercept b with the x-intercept (where the line crosses the x-axis).
misconception_checks.correction: b is specifically the y-coordinate when x = 0 — it is read off the y-axis, not the x-axis. The x-intercept is a different point and is not part of y = mx + b directly.
misconception_checks.graph_evidence: On y = 2x + 3, b = 3 is at (0, 3) on the y-axis. The x-intercept is at (-1.5, 0) — a completely different location.

misconception_checks.misconception: A larger signed value of m always means a steeper line (e.g., students think m = 4 is steeper than m = -7).
misconception_checks.correction: Steepness is determined by the absolute value |m|. A line with m = -7 is steeper than one with m = 4 because |-7| = 7 > |4| = 4. The sign tells you direction (up or down), not steepness.
misconception_checks.graph_evidence: Plotting y = 4x + 3 and y = -7x + 3 side by side shows y = -7x + 3 is visibly more tilted from horizontal, even though its m is negative.

misconception_checks.misconception: Students assume that if two lines share the same m they must be identical, or that changing m automatically changes b.
misconception_checks.correction: m and b are independent parameters. Two lines can share the same slope (making them parallel) while having different y-intercepts, or share the same y-intercept while having different slopes. Neither forces the other to change.
misconception_checks.graph_evidence: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x + 5 are parallel (same m, different b). y = 2x + 3 and y = 5x + 3 cross at (0, 3) (same b, different m).

misconception_checks.misconception: Students try to write a vertical line such as x = 4 in the form y = mx + b by assigning m a very large number.
misconception_checks.correction: A vertical line has Δx = 0 between any two points on it. Since m = Δy/Δx and division by zero is undefined, no finite value of m can represent a vertical line. Vertical lines must be written as x = c.
misconception_checks.graph_evidence: Attempting to compute slope for x = 4 using points (4, 0) and (4, 3): Δx = 0, so Δy/Δx = 3/0, which is undefined — no number can fill that slot.
